stories.headline: Bill for Birmingham's Oracle debacle reaches £128M
stories.claim: Birmingham City Council's Oracle finance system overhaul now costs £128.1m, over six times the 2019 estimate.
stories.summary: Birmingham City Council faces a bill of £128.1 million for its troubled move from SAP to Oracle, more than six times the £19.96 million forecast in the 2019 business case. A report to the council's Audit Committee this week gave the combined cost of the original 2022 implementation and this year's reimplementation, and said the new Oracle Fusion system went live in August without any priority-one issues. The first attempt, which went live in April 2022, caused serious problems, including failed bank reconciliation, an inability to produce auditable accounts and over £5 million spent on manual workarounds. The disaster is widely linked to the council's effective bankruptcy. The Register says the true cost is likely higher once lost savings and tax collection problems are counted, with one 2024 estimate reaching £216.5 million.
key_points: The reimplementation and original rollout together cost £128.1 million, against a £19.96 million forecast in 2019.
The project's funding allocation had previously reached £157 million, according to the programme report.

stories.headline: Ford unveils GT41 Le Mans hypercar for 2027 World Endurance Championship
stories.claim: Ford has unveiled the GT41 LMDh hypercar, which will return to the FIA World Endurance Championship top class in 2027.
stories.summary: Ford has unveiled the GT41, a new hypercar that marks its 2027 return to the top class of the FIA World Endurance Championship and the 24 Hours of Le Mans. The car was revealed at Detroit's Ford Field during the Thanksgiving Day football game on 26 November 2026, exactly 60 years after Ford's 1966 Le Mans one-two-three finish. It uses the LMDh formula, with an Oreca carbon chassis and standard hybrid parts, while Ford supplies a 5.4-litre V8 derived from the Mustang's Coyote engine and the hybrid control software. The programme starts in Qatar in March 2027, the first of nine WEC rounds, with Le Mans following in June. Ford is not entering the IMSA series, so the GT41 will not race at Daytona in January. The Hypercar class is highly competitive, with Toyota the reigning Le Mans and title winner after three years of Ferrari dominance.

stories.headline: Global Brands Shift $250 Million in Orders From Bangladesh Amid Unrest
stories.claim: Global brands reportedly moved about $250m of garment orders out of Bangladesh to India and other Asian hubs amid unrest.
stories.summary: Global fashion retailers have reportedly shifted around $254m of orders away from Bangladesh, mainly to India, after labour unrest and rising costs. The diversion took place between 1 and 18 November and equals nearly a tenth of the country's monthly garment orders. Zara, H&M, Marks & Spencer and Celio are among the brands named by factory owners. The trigger was a 36% rise in the garment minimum wage, the smallest in four decades, which fell short of workers' demands to more than double pay and sparked fresh clashes with police. The BGMEA estimates protests have caused over $400m in production losses. Indian textile shares rose, with Gokaldas Exports up as much as 11%. Garments make up more than 80% of Bangladesh's export earnings.

stories.headline: Americans Are Making Political Statements With Their Spending
stories.claim: A new survey finds US shoppers increasingly let companies' political stances influence what they buy.
stories.summary: US shoppers are increasingly letting politics shape what they buy, according to a new survey of 1,115 Americans by Goods Unite Us and SmartCustomer, conducted about four weeks before the 3 November midterms. Some 67 percent said a company's political affiliation influences their purchases to a significant degree, up sharply from 2024. Boycotts have roughly doubled: 51 percent said they had boycotted a firm over its politics in the past year, against 30 percent in 2024. The survey also found that 53 percent want companies to be more open about their political positions, while only 22 percent think they should stay private. The findings suggest brands face rising pressure to take clearer public stances.
key_points: 67 percent of US shoppers rate a company's political affiliation as a significant factor in purchases, up from a minority in 2024.
51 percent said they boycotted a company over its politics in the past 12 months, compared with 30 percent in 2024.
64 percent of Democratic-leaning and 47 percent of Republican-leaning shoppers said they had boycotted a firm.
Only 22 percent now think companies should keep political positions private, down from 41 percent in 2024.
64 percent would pay more for an equal-quality product from a company whose politics match their own.
The survey was run by Goods Unite Us and SmartCustomer, with a sample of 1,115 US shoppers.
stories.market_take: Consumer boycott pressure could weigh on brands seen as politically polarising, though the survey is small and self-reported.

stories.headline: Dutch Groups Ask Court to Halt Meta AI Glasses Sales on Privacy Concerns
stories.claim: Two Dutch consumer groups have asked an Amsterdam court to halt Meta smart glasses sales in the Netherlands over privacy.
stories.summary: Two Dutch groups, Consumentenbond and Offlimits, asked the Amsterdam District Court on 26 November 2026 to stop Meta and EssilorLuxottica selling Meta AI smart glasses to Dutch consumers. They argue the glasses let wearers film people without their knowledge, which they say could breach European privacy law. The plaintiffs also want Meta to build in protections against covert filming and to stop using such recordings to train its AI models. Any ruling would apply only in the Netherlands, though it could set a wider European precedent. No hearing date or timetable has been reported, and the case is at a very early stage.

stories.claim: Puig has agreed to pay €1.2 billion in cash for Advent International's 75% stake in Artessence, owner of Parfums de Marly and Initio.

An arrest warrant has also been issued for news coordinator Kürşad Oğuz, who is reported to be abroad. The channel's headquarters was raided last month, its live broadcasts were halted and a government-appointed administrator took over. The move follows the seizure of Sozcu TV earlier this month and adds to a wider crackdown on critics of President Erdoğan, including the jailing of his main rival, Istanbul mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu.

Universal Credit, pensions, PIP applications and the Tell Us Once bereavement service are among those affected, leaving claimants unable to log in to their accounts. The DWP says benefit and pension payments are unaffected and will be paid as normal, and claimants will not be sanctioned for missed online uploads. Downing Street has not ruled out a cyber attack but says there is no evidence personal data has been lost, and officials say no other government departments appear affected. The DWP processes about 2.5 million payments a day, worth around £1.3bn. The shutdown was taken as a precaution, and the BBC has compared it with the Co-op hack last year, where a precautionary shutdown proved too late. The cause and scale remain unclear.

stories.headline: S&P cuts France credit outlook to negative, keeping A+ rating
stories.claim: S&P has revised France's sovereign outlook to negative from stable while affirming its A+ rating.
stories.summary: S&P Global has moved its outlook on France's sovereign credit rating to negative from stable, signalling that a downgrade could follow, while affirming the A+/A-1 rating itself. The agency expects larger fiscal deficits this year and next than it previously forecast, citing weak growth, higher interest costs and political polarisation that could persist beyond the 2027 presidential election. The move comes as France's 10-year borrowing costs rose above 5.14% in October, their highest since 2002, and official Insee data showed the economy contracted 0.2% in the third quarter, more than first thought, a technical recession. The minority government, led by Finance Minister Roland Lescure, wants to cut the deficit from 5.4% of output this year to 5.0% in 2027, but parliament is deeply divided. Lescure said the government remains committed to fiscal consolidation. Markets will watch whether the 2027 budget passes, and whether rival raters Moody's or Fitch follow.

Flight 638, bound for Dallas-Fort Worth, struck the wing of Flight 2152, bound for Chicago O'Hare. No injuries were reported, and a broken wingtip piece was reportedly seen on the ground. Both aircraft returned to the gate and were removed from service for inspection by American's maintenance team, and passengers were to be rebooked on other planes. The FAA said it will investigate. The incident is especially sensitive at the airport, where a January 2025 midair collision with an Army helicopter killed 67 people, and the NTSB later blamed systemic failures, including FAA decisions on helicopter operations. It also follows several similar tarmac wingtip strikes in the US in recent weeks.
key_points: Two American Airlines Boeing 737s made wingtip contact while taxiing at Reagan National on Friday evening, around 5:10pm ET.
Flight 638 to Dallas struck Flight 2152 to Chicago; no injuries were reported.

stories.headline: U.K. Regulator Says McCormick Sale of Colman’s Could Address Unilever Foods Merger Concerns
stories.claim: UK regulator says McCormick's planned sale of Colman's could address concerns over its $65bn Unilever foods merger.
stories.summary: Britain's Competition and Markets Authority has said that McCormick's proposed sale of Unilever's Colman's brand could in principle resolve its concerns about the $65 billion merger of Unilever's foods business with McCormick. The CMA had warned earlier this month that competition in recipe mixes and sauces could be reduced, threatening an in-depth investigation. It found that Nestlé's Maggi, Premier Foods' Bisto and supermarket own-label products offer only limited competition to the merged group in supplying dry ingredients and sauce mixes to UK retailers. The regulator will now examine the remedy in more detail, including seeking feedback from third parties, and must approve any buyer. Unilever launched the Colman's sale in August and declined to give financial details. The deal, which would combine Knorr and Hellmann's with McCormick, is described as the second-largest food transaction in history.

stories.headline: Can AI crack encryption?
stories.claim: OpenAI released 722 AI-written math papers, prompting cryptographers to debate whether AI could weaken public-key encryption.
stories.summary: OpenAI published 722 mathematical manuscripts written by an unreleased AI model, a release that has unsettled cryptographers. Three papers were withdrawn within a day, and mathematicians are still checking the rest. Cryptography underpins secure messaging and bank log-ins, and its security depends on maths problems believed to be intractable. Johns Hopkins cryptographer Matthew Green put the chance that confidence in existing public-key algorithms could be lost at 15%. He pointed to the number field sieve, which made RSA easier to break at 512-bit keys, prompting longer keys. Elliptic curve cryptography, used widely on the internet and by cryptocurrencies, could also be vulnerable if AI finds shortcuts. Researchers caution that the risk is speculative for now.
key_points: OpenAI released 722 math papers last week, all produced by an AI model not available to the public.

Matthew Green estimated a 15% chance that public-key encryption confidence could be lost.
Precedent: a number field sieve advance forced RSA keys to lengthen to 2,048 bits.

Worries focus on banking and commerce data leak risks.

stories.headline: GTA in Istanbul? Meet the game developers bringing virtual crime chaos to their home cities

stories.summary: A wave of small, independent studios is building Grand Theft Auto-style sandbox games set in their own home cities, from a Manchester council estate to 1970s Istanbul and Helsinki. stories.headline: EU leaders fail to agree 2028-34 budget as talks collapse; resume in December
stories.claim: EU leaders ended a 12-hour Brussels summit without agreeing the 2028-34 budget; talks resume at a summit on 17-18 December.
stories.summary: EU leaders ended a 12-hour Brussels summit on Thursday without agreeing the 2028-34 long-term budget, and talks will resume at a summit on 17 and 18 December. The main fault line runs between France and Italy, which want higher spending, and Germany and other fiscally cautious members, which want cuts of roughly €220bn to €230bn from the €2tn Commission proposal. Council President António Costa's current proposal totals €1.582tn, including €140bn to repay pandemic-era borrowing, and it cuts €44bn from an earlier plan. Talks also stalled over a €45bn (£37.6bn) loan to Ukraine, which Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Hungary oppose, while Germany is pressing four countries to help repay the borrowing. Merz said there was "new movement" toward smaller budgets but that the bloc was not there yet, and Macron called lower spending a strategic mistake. Because unanimous approval from all 27 states is required, the outcome remains uncertain, and the proposal includes five new EU taxes worth €60bn a year that leaders have yet to approve.

stories.headline: Thanksgiving storm cuts power to nearly a million homes and postpones Macy's parade
stories.claim: A Thanksgiving storm left nearly a million homes without power and forced Macy's to postpone its parade, with about 260,000 still out on Friday evening.
stories.summary: A powerful Thanksgiving storm battered the US East Coast, Mid-Atlantic and Midwest, with outages peaking near one million on Thursday night. By Friday evening more than 260,000 customers were still without power, down from over 360,000 earlier that day. Pennsylvania, Virginia, Maryland and New Jersey were worst affected, and New Jersey and New York declared states of emergency. Macy's postponed its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday 28 November at 8.30am, its first postponement in its history apart from three wartime years. Flight disruption was heavy, with more than 3,400 delays and nearly 670 cancellations on Friday alone, after more than 400 cancellations on Thursday. Central Park recorded its wettest Thanksgiving on record. President Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds for the East Coast, and record king tides also hit California. Forecasters expect a drier weekend in the north-east, but another low-pressure system is due on Monday.

stories.summary: New Zealand's ruling right-wing coalition has lost its parliamentary majority after official final results from the 7 November election, leaving Prime Minister Christopher Luxon dependent on the centrist Opportunity Party. National won 40 seats, ACT 13 and NZ First 12, one short of the 65 needed in the 130-seat parliament, after losing two seats between the preliminary and final counts due to special votes. Opportunity, led by Qiulae Wong, won seven seats and 6.1% of the vote and now holds the balance of power. Wong has set non-negotiable conditions on climate action, cost of living and political reform, and has ruled out Winston Peters serving as foreign minister. Labour won 36 seats, so a left-led government lacks the numbers even with Opportunity's support. Luxon, who had ruled out working with Opportunity, now says he needs its support, and both he and Labour leader Chris Hipkins have held lengthy meetings with Wong. Officials say talks could take weeks or months, and a fresh election is possible if no deal is struck. The election was dominated by inflation and access to healthcare concerns.

Washington accuses Beijing of falling short on farm purchases and rare earths, while China has extended its suspension of a critical minerals export ban until 27 January. Goldman Sachs estimates the EU at 15%, Vietnam up to 20% or 35% without a deal, and India at 25%. A USTR hearing on 25 January points to implementation around late February or March, and footwear makers warn the costs will fall on American consumers.

stories.headline: Higher Fuel Costs Weigh on Apparel Retail Earnings
stories.claim: US apparel and discount retailers report margin pressure from fuel and freight costs tied to the Iran war, with mixed guidance changes.
stories.summary: Higher fuel costs linked to the Iran war are squeezing US apparel and discount retailers, and their latest results show a split picture. Burlington cut its full-year adjusted EPS outlook to $11.70 to $11.80 after taking a $17 million fourth-quarter hit, while Dollar Tree raised its guidance to $8.05 to $8.25. Abercrombie and Kohl's lifted their outlooks, but Gap lowered its own. Diesel averaged $5.95 a gallon from August to October and was $5.695 in late November, still about 49.5% above pre-war levels. Ross Stores is the clearest example: third-quarter sales rose 12% to $6.26 billion, yet its shares fell 2.92% to $213.46 after it guided to a slower holiday quarter. The episode shows how energy costs are feeding through to US consumer retail margins heading into the key holiday season.

Ross guided to 4% to 5% holiday same-store sales growth, down from last year's 9%, and its CFO said higher freight costs were already hitting margins.

stories.claim: US Thanksgiving meal costs are rising again, with the American Farm Bureau estimating a more than 6% increase.
stories.summary: The cost of a traditional US Thanksgiving dinner is rising again, with the American Farm Bureau Federation estimating it will be more than 6% higher than last year. Staples such as cranberries and dinner rolls are pushing up the total, although the Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute expects the average food bill to be slightly cheaper than last year thanks to promotions. Grocery prices have risen nearly 22% over five years, according to federal data, which economists link to wars in Ukraine and Iran, US tariffs and severe weather. A LendingTree survey found 53% of respondents said inflation was affecting their holiday plans, and fewer people expect to host guests this year, at 51% compared with 59% last year. The picture is mixed, but it matters for household budgets and for the Federal Reserve, which watches food prices in its inflation assessment.

stories.headline: UK to pay 4% 'participation' fee on top of contributions under reset EU deals
stories.claim: The UK will pay the EU a 4% 'participation fee' on top of its main contribution under the reset deals agreed by PM Andy Burnham.
stories.summary: Britain will pay the EU a 4% "participation fee" on top of its operational contribution under the deals agreed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, according to treaty texts published this week. The main payment, made in euros, is scaled to the size of the UK economy relative to the EU, and the fee covers running costs of three EU agencies and systems needed for the food standards and carbon trading agreements. Officials estimate the extra costs at low tens of millions of pounds a year and say economic gains will far outweigh them, though no full total estimate has been published. The deals cover food standards alignment and re-linking to the EU carbon trading regime, and are due to take effect in 2028. A youth visa agreement for 18 to 31 year olds is expected to be published in coming days. Opposition leaders Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage criticised the deals, with Badenoch attacking the government's broad powers to adopt EU law without full votes.

stories.headline: Japan's upper house rejects censure motion against scandal-hit minister Seki
stories.claim: Japan's upper house rejected a non-binding censure motion against Education Minister Yoshihiro Seki, 124 votes to 120, letting PM Takaichi keep him in post.
stories.summary: Japan's upper house narrowly voted down a non-binding censure motion against Education Minister Yoshihiro Seki on Friday 27 November, by 124 votes to 120. The motion, filed by seven opposition parties and one parliamentary group, targeted Seki for inviting government officials to political fundraising parties he hosted in 2024, where attendees paid 90,000 yen each, including representatives of biopharmaceutical companies. Seki first told parliament officials attended only two events, then admitted three more had also been attended by officials from the Japan Fair Trade Commission and the Cabinet Office. The result lets Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi keep him in post despite calls for his resignation and gives the government breathing space. Opposition parties had threatened to boycott deliberations on a consumption tax cut bill that Takaichi wants passed before an April start, and the government needs opposition votes in the upper house. The Diet session ends on 12 December, and the scandal could still resurface.

stories.summary: An uncontrolled bushfire on Flinders Island in Tasmania has burned roughly 14,500 hectares, about a tenth of the island, with flames reaching 10 metres. stories.headline: Faisal Islam: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat
stories.claim: Trump's new tariff announcement this week is seen as a tentative legal fix rather than a fresh trade shock, with rates due from January or February.
stories.summary: The latest Trump tariff package has arrived with little of the drama of last April's 'Liberation Day', and analysts read it as an effort to shore up the legal basis for the duties rather than a shift in trade policy. The new tariffs are not due to take effect until January or February, the rates are upper ceilings open to negotiation, and the US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has talked of a broad plurilateral talks on excess capacity. The tariffs rest on two legal bases after the Supreme Court struck down the original emergency powers earlier this year, and 25 states are challenging the forced labour tariffs in court. China's rate stays at 20% under last year's truce, which expires in mid-January, while Canada faces Section 338 duties that Democrats want to repeal. Economists now expect some of the tariffs to remain for years, and the G20 summit in Miami next month will be a key test.
key_points: The new tariffs are due to start in January or February after a consultation period, and the stated rates are ceilings that remain open to negotiation.
The Supreme Court struck down the original emergency-powers basis earlier this year, so the administration now relies on two legal foundations, including forced labour provisions.
The UK is not hit by the new announcements but still faces an extra 10% under the forced labour provisions, and no action was taken on its digital services tax.
China's tariff stays at 20% under the truce, which expires in mid-January, and Beijing has responded with restraint rather than retaliation.
Over half of the tariffs on Canada rest on Section 338 of the Smoot-Hawley Act, and a Senate bill to repeal them has been introduced, though the incoming Democratic House majority has limited power.
China's exports have been rerouted, with the US share falling to around 10% this year from 15% two years ago.
stories.market_take: Tariffs are set to arrive later and at lower-than-feared intensity, though some duties may last for years, which keeps trade-exposed exporters on watch.

stories.summary: Sarah Breeden, the Bank of England's deputy governor, has warned that AI has turned cyber attacks into a systemic risk for the financial system. Speaking at the Institute of International Finance annual meeting in Bangkok, she said banks can no longer assume attackers will not get through and need bare-metal recovery options for core services. The BoE is surveying lenders on their readiness for quantum computing threats to encryption and will use the findings to shape a system-wide response. Her chief worries are hostile states or hackers weaponising advanced AI, and rogue AI agents bypassing safeguards. The headline indicates the central bank plans to cut capital requirements, but the available text covers only the cyber warnings, so the capital move is not detailed here. The source article is dated 26 November, while the reproduced PYMNTS text refers to remarks on 15 October, so the timing is unclear.
key_points: Deputy Governor Sarah Breeden said AI now makes cyber attacks a systemic risk for the financial system.
Banks should plan for bare-metal recovery so core services can run if primary systems are compromised.
The BoE is surveying lenders on their preparedness for quantum computing threats to encryption.
Breeden's main worries are hostile states or hackers weaponising AI, and rogue AI agents bypassing safeguards.
The headline says the BoE will cut capital requirements, but the available text does not give the details.
stories.market_take: Banks may see lighter capital requirements, though the text does not give the scale of any cut.

stories.headline: UK privacy watchdog faces probe into its workplace culture
stories.claim: An independent review will examine the culture and governance of the UK's data watchdog after John Edwards' resignation.
stories.summary: Britain's privacy regulator is to face an independent review into its culture, governance and accountability, led by Karon Monaghan KC. The review follows the resignation of former Information Commissioner John Edwards in June, after an investigation found a case to answer over his conduct. That inquiry looked only at Edwards, so the new review will examine whether staff could raise concerns and what happened to those who did. It will not reopen the Edwards investigation or examine named individuals. The Information Commission replaced the old ICO on 30 September, and DCMS Secretary Lisa Nandy said the government wants to find what needs to change. Monaghan is expected to report in the first quarter of 2027.
key_points: Karon Monaghan KC will lead an independent review of the ICO's culture, governance and accountability.

stories.headline: 'Significant number of customer records' pwned in Flight Centre Travel Group breach
stories.claim: Flight Centre Travel Group says a significant number of customer records may have been accessed in a third-party booking system breach.
stories.summary: Australian travel giant Flight Centre Travel Group has disclosed to the ASX that a cyberattack on a third-party accommodation booking system may have exposed a significant number of customer records. The system is used by Flight Centre, Travel Associates, Cruiseabout and some independent agents. Initial review suggests most records hold only names, with a very small share containing birth dates, emails, limited passport details, phone numbers or, rarely, health or mobility information. The company has contained the attack, rotated keys and is working with supplier and Mandiant, and says flight and corporate bookings are unaffected. The breach follows similar attacks on Booking.com and BWH Hotels, and on RMS Cloud, which led to WhatsApp scams in October.

stories.headline: X finally launches parental controls for teen accounts
stories.claim: X has launched parental controls letting parents of teen accounts set limits and monitor contacts without reading private messages.
stories.summary: X has rolled out parental controls for teen accounts, giving guardians a view of weekly time spent, the power to set daily limits and to approve new followers. Parents can also restrict For You recommendations, filter words, block sensitive media and manage who can send direct messages. They cannot read private messages, see searches or viewing history, or post as the teen. One guardian can supervise up to five teen accounts, and both sides must agree before supervision starts. It ends automatically when the teen turns adult. X's head of safety, Michael O'Herlihy, framed the tools as guardrails rather than surveillance.

stories.headline: Canada adds C$700M to its AI compute fund, favouring home-grown clouds
stories.claim: Canada is adding C$700M to its AI Compute Access Fund, lifting it to C$1bn and favouring Canadian-owned computing.
stories.summary: Canada is more than tripling its AI Compute Access Fund, adding C$700m to take it to C$1bn from C$300m, with larger subsidies for firms that use Canadian-owned and run computing. The announcement came on Thursday from Evan Solomon, the minister of artificial intelligence and digital innovation. A first new funding round targets health and life sciences projects. Solomon also confirmed more than C$52m for 45 firms from the fund's first phase, bringing its total to over C$118m for 89 companies. The money sits under Canada's national AI strategy from June, and Ottawa is also bringing 500 megawatts of its own AI computing online. The move aims to build demand for domestic cloud providers.

stories.headline: Rackspace pulls plug on Spot cloud service after security breach
stories.claim: Rackspace is shutting its low-cost Spot cloud service on 8 December after a credential-based security breach.
stories.summary: Rackspace is shutting down its low-cost Spot cloud service after a security breach, giving customers roughly two weeks to move workloads and retrieve data. The service ceases operations on December 8 at 2300 UTC, after which any running workloads will be terminated. Attackers used leaked credentials to access parts of Spot for almost 22 hours on November 17, impersonating users, planting pods in customer Kubernetes clusters and reaching stored secrets. Rackspace only found out the following day after a customer raised the alarm. Customers must reissue API tokens, download new configuration files and rotate database passwords and third-party keys. Rackspace has not explained why it chose closure over recovery or how many customers were hit.

stories.headline: The Ellisons’ debt-fuelled takeover of Hollywood
stories.claim: Skydance, formed from Paramount and Warner Bros, carries about $80bn of net debt after a record $110bn merger.
stories.summary: David Ellison's Paramount has closed a $110bn (£82bn) merger with Warner Bros, now rebranded as Skydance, and the company carries roughly $80bn of net debt, around seven times profits. That is almost three times the 2.5x leverage usually associated with the industry, according to Enders Analysis. Servicing the debt will cost about $5.8bn a year. Paramount raised $52bn of debt in a week to close the deal, the largest leveraged buyout in history, and the timing coincided with a wider bond sell-off that has pushed up borrowing costs. The combined group owns Harry Potter, Game of Thrones, HBO Max, Paramount+, CNN and CBS. Analysts warn that deep cost cuts will be needed to reduce leverage and satisfy investors. The Financial Times piece itself was only available as a headline, so the details come from The Telegraph's reporting.

stories.headline: Shares find footing after bruising month, dollar set for third monthly gain
stories.claim: Asian shares steady to end a bruising November as the dollar heads for a third monthly gain on Fed hike bets.
stories.summary: Asian shares were set to end a painful November on a steadier note, with the US dollar rising towards its third straight monthly gain as traders bet heavily on a Federal Reserve rate rise in December. Futures implied a 99% chance of a Fed hike, while the dollar index was up 1.8% for the month at 103.8. Japan's Nikkei rose 0.7% but still lost 8.4% in November, and MSCI's Asia-Pacific ex-Japan index was down 8.2% for the month. Oil was set for its first weekly rise in four weeks, with Brent at US$96.14 a barrel, though it fell 18% in November. Data showed Tokyo core inflation hit a 16-month high, strengthening the case for a Bank of Japan hike as soon as December. Nvidia faced unease after S&P placed its credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade, and reports said it had told partners to stop shipping chip-containing servers to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia.

stories.headline: UK auto production rises 4.8% from a year ago in October, SMMT data shows
stories.claim: UK car and vehicle production rose in October, with exports surging as car output recovered from last year's JLR cyber attack.
stories.summary: British vehicle production rose 4.8% year on year in October to 64,141 units, according to the SMMT. Car output climbed for a third straight month, up 6.2% to 61,746, helped by a recovery after a cyber incident halted Jaguar Land Rover last year. Car exports jumped 14.2%, with shipments to the US up 70.9% while EU shipments fell 7.1%. Exports made up 82.6% of car production, the highest share since December 2024. Year-to-date production is still down 2.3% at 628,678 units. The SMMT warned about the EU's proposed Made in Europe rules and post-Brexit origin rules from 2027, and EU diplomats reportedly lean towards including British EVs in the scheme.

stories.headline: Asia made a big AI bet on Nvidia. What happens now?
stories.claim: Huang's return as Nvidia boss sent Asian tech markets on a volatile ride, exposing the region's heavy reliance on Nvidia and AI.

Analysts say the region is now deeply tied to Nvidia's fortunes, with Taiwan's TSMC making most of its chips, Samsung and SK Hynix supplying memory, and Nvidia acting as a major lender to AI supply-chain firms. Asia-Pacific data-centre investment hit a record $11.6bn (£8.85bn) in 2025, and big tech firms plan to lift regional infrastructure spending by about 60% this year. The region is also exposed to new US export rules, announced last week, that tighten scrutiny of data-centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil. Nvidia has reportedly paused shipments to the region, and Huang is due to testify before Congress next week.

stories.headline: MIT’s Robot Builds a Sleeve Around an Arm Without a Stitch
stories.claim: MIT Media Lab robot arm draws a fitted sleeve directly onto a forearm using heated plastic thread.
stories.summary: A robotic arm at the MIT Media Lab can build a sleeve directly around a person's forearm, drawing fine threads of softened plastic until the garment forms in place. The InSituWear project, led by the Critical Matter Group under Behnaz Farahi with research lead Sergio Mutis, skips body scanning, digital pattern-making and seam assembly. The team described the method in an April 2026 paper, showing a sleeve and a glove. A roughly 14-inch sleeve took 22 minutes to make, but durability, comfort over a full day and wrapping flat or recessed areas remain open problems. The approach is an early research step rather than a product, though it hints at custom-fit wearables made with little waste.
key_points: MIT Media Lab's Critical Matter Group built InSituWear, a robot that wraps plastic thread around a person's arm to form a fitted sleeve.
The method uses a heated needle to pull threads from polycaprolactone, a plastic that softens at low temperatures and sticks where strands overlap.
A paper published in April 2026 showed a sleeve and a glove; the sleeve took 22 minutes to make.
Varying strand thickness, spacing and crossing angle lets designers make some areas firmer and others more flexible.
The glove changes colour via heat-sensitive pigment when a circuit closes, but still needs a battery and wiring.
Long-term wear comfort, repeated flexing and end-of-life recyclability have not yet been tested.

Inspired by ancient Roman mosaics and pottery seen in Pompeii, he hand-carves vessels in marble and pairs them with rock crystal, smoky quartz and citrine quartz. Kolodziejczak, who began as a jewellery designer for Givenchy and Saint Laurent, says he treats furniture like jewellery, aiming for single extraordinary accents rather than room-filling pieces. The exhibition is a good example of how craft and material reuse are reaching the high-end design market.

stories.headline: Supermodel Veruschka, 1960s icon, dies at 87
stories.claim: German-born supermodel Veruschka, a 1960s icon, has died at 87, Bild confirmed on 25 November.
stories.summary: Veruschka, the German-born supermodel known for her shape-shifting presence and body art, has died aged 87, according to Bild, which confirmed the news on 25 November. She died at home surrounded by friends and family. Born Vera von Lehndorff-Steinort in Königsberg in 1939, she was discovered in Florence in 1959 and became one of the first supermodels, appearing on 13 American Vogue covers and on the British Vogue cover in February 1969. She worked with Richard Avedon, Irving Penn, Horst P. Horst and David Bailey, and played a version of herself in Michelangelo Antonioni's 1966 film Blow-Up. Later she turned to art photography with Holger Trülzsch and made occasional runway returns, including for Chanel in 1994 and Giles Deacon in 2011. Her childhood was marked by the Nazi regime, after her father was executed following the 1944 plot against Hitler.

stories.claim: The MoD has written to about 100,000 strategic reservists and recent veterans to prepare for possible call-up, but reportedly lacks working contact details for about half.
stories.summary: The Ministry of Defence has written to about 100,000 strategic reservists and recently departed veterans, telling them to be ready for a possible call-up, the first such move since the Cold War. The letters, signed by the chiefs of all three armed services, invite volunteers for training such as Nato's Steadfast Defender exercise next spring and ask recipients to update their contact details, current jobs and skills. The MoD says the aim is to strengthen deterrence and improve data on former personnel, and insists no mobilisation is being suggested. The Telegraph now reports that the department cannot contact about half of the reservists because of administrative errors, leaving tens of thousands unlikely to receive the letters. The government says the recall threshold is high and would apply only to serious emergencies or preparations for war, while Lord Robertson and Air Chief Marshal Sir Richard Knighton have warned the UK lacks an effective system for tracking recent leavers. The move follows Russian cruise missiles and a drone entering eastern Poland, and the British Army has about 73,000 active personnel, its smallest since the Napoleonic Wars.

The MoD reportedly lacks working addresses for about half of the reservists.
The government says the recall threshold is high and no mobilisation is being suggested.
Lord Robertson and Air Chief Marshal Sir Richard Knighton have warned about poor tracking of recent leavers.

stories.headline: Airline Norse Atlantic says financial situation 'critical,' shares plunge
stories.claim: Norway's Norse Atlantic says its finances are 'critical' and it needs short-term financing; shares plunge 85%.
stories.summary: Norse Atlantic, the Norwegian long-haul budget airline, has said its financial situation is "critical" and that it needs new financing to meet short-term liquidity needs. Its shares closed down 85% on Wednesday, hitting an all-time low and wiping out most of the market value it had left this year. The carrier blamed soaring jet fuel costs linked to the US-Israeli war with Iran and the disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, and it does not hedge its fuel. It has cut capacity, furloughed crew and suspended unprofitable routes, and it launched a formal sale or merger process in July. It did not say how long it can operate without new money. The squeeze is hitting Europe's weaker carriers hard, with airBaltic in Chapter 11 and EasyJet's sale to Apollo Global Management in train.

stories.headline: Judge blocks FCC early review of Disney's ABC licences, likely violating First Amendment
stories.claim: A federal judge blocked the FCC's early review of Disney's eight ABC station licences, finding it likely violates the First Amendment.
stories.summary: A federal judge in Washington has blocked the Federal Communications Commission from carrying out an early review of licences for eight ABC-owned stations, finding the move likely violates the First Amendment. Judge Loren AliKhan granted Disney and ABC a preliminary injunction and temporary restraining order, and refused the FCC's motion to dismiss the lawsuit. She wrote that the review was no coincidence, noting it began the day after Jimmy Kimmel joked about Melania Trump, and cited eleven occasions on which President Trump urged the FCC to strip ABC's licences. The FCC announced the review in April, even though most of the licences run until 2030 or 2031, and ordered the stations to submit renewals years early. The affected cities include New York, Los Angeles and Chicago. The judge declined to bar all formal or informal FCC pressure, saying ABC had not specified what those might be. The FCC, led by Brendan Carr, says the ruling is wrong and expects to prevail, arguing the review is part of a diversity-hiring inquiry.

stories.headline: FCC conditionally approves SpaceX plan for up to one million orbital data center satellites
stories.claim: The FCC conditionally approved SpaceX's plan for a constellation of up to one million satellites for orbital data centres.
stories.summary: The US Federal Communications Commission has given SpaceX conditional approval to deploy and operate a constellation of up to one million satellites for an orbital data centre business, a decision taken on Wednesday. The approval is a regulatory win for Elon Musk's plan to move AI computing into space, despite objections from Amazon, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society over debris, interference and environmental effects. The FCC set aside some of those concerns as outside its remit, and the order sets conditions on interference with US government systems in the 28.6-29.1 GHz band. It also deferred a decision on SpaceX's request to waive rules on satellite disposal, saying the company had not provided enough detail. SpaceX still needs further approvals, including a debris plan for satellites above 600 km, and has seven years to get its first satellite operational and 14 years to complete the constellation. Technical and funding hurdles, such as cooling chips in orbit and cutting launch costs, remain large, and critics note the economics are unproven.

He is the fourth Politburo member investigated since 2025, after He Weidong, Zhang Youxia and Ma Xingrui, extending Xi Jinping's sweeping crackdown that has thinned China's senior leadership and military command. Shanghai's party paper pledged loyalty to Xi and said the anti-corruption campaign would not slow. Analysts say the probe deepens upheaval before the 2027 leadership reshuffle, and investors will watch for any effect on policy continuity in Shanghai, China's financial hub.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO after Trump push; investigations and governance questions linger
stories.claim: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on 23 November after Trump pressed for his return; probes and congressional scrutiny continue.
stories.summary: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, president and director with immediate effect on 23 November, less than two weeks after he resigned on 12 November. The board said US government input indicated his return poses no national security risk and that it was satisfied with his candour and ability to lead. Trump said he 'made the deal' by pressing the board, and VP JD Vance reportedly held a private call with Huang and reassured directors. Nvidia shares closed about 31% higher, adding nearly $1tn in market value, and the Nasdaq rose about 6.4%. Huang had stepped down after admitting an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive whom US intelligence has reportedly linked to a Chinese espionage network. Shares then fell 8.5% on Tuesday and remain about 37% below their October peak, and four congressional committees have asked Huang to testify while the SEC, Justice Department and an independent board probe continue. The episode matters because Nvidia is the world's most valuable chipmaker and its governance is now under political and legal scrutiny.
key_points: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, president and director with immediate effect on 23 November.
The board said US government input indicated his return poses no national security risk.
Nvidia shares closed about 31% higher on Monday, adding nearly $1tn in market value, and the Nasdaq rose about 6.4%.
Shares fell about 8.5% on Tuesday and were still down 37% from their early-October peak, according to later reports.
Huang faces questioning before four congressional committees, including a closed-door meeting with three House committees on 1 December, and he will speak at GTC Washington.
The SEC, Department of Justice and an independent board probe into security and IP leakage continue, and Senator Elizabeth Warren has demanded answers.
stories.market_take: Investors see Huang's return as a sign of continuity for Nvidia, which is a bellwether for the AI chip trade.

Google is pursuing a similar approach with Private AI Compute. Business data is already excluded from training, unlike consumer ChatGPT conversations.

stories.headline: ESA's Hera probe finds DART left a stadium-sized crater on asteroid Dimorphos
stories.claim: ESA's Hera probe shows NASA's DART impact left a stadium-sized crater on asteroid Dimorphos, which now tumbles in orbit.
stories.summary: The European Space Agency's Hera probe has sent back its first close views of the aftermath of NASA's 2022 DART impact on Dimorphos, the moon of asteroid Didymos. The images show a crater roughly the size of a sports stadium, stretching across nearly the asteroid's entire 151-metre width, and the body now tumbles in its orbit instead of keeping one face toward Didymos. Hera also identified more than 100 boulders in a debris field larger than the team expected. Scientists had predicted a crater of about 20 metres, and the orbit was shortened by 33 minutes and 15 seconds, far beyond NASA's 73-second target, suggesting debris amplified the push. Hera will move from 25-30 km to about 13 km for higher-resolution imaging, and two CubeSats, Juventas and Milani, are due to deploy in early 2027 to attempt landings and collect data. The mission is slated to last six months. The results will refine models of how effectively a spacecraft can deflect a dangerous asteroid.

Dimorphos now tumbles in its orbit rather than keeping one face toward its partner Didymos.

stories.headline: Too Much, Too Little: Bangladesh’s Wage Hike Pleases No One
stories.claim: Bangladesh's wage board raised the garment minimum wage 36% to 17,000 taka, a hike unions and brands both criticise.
stories.summary: Bangladesh has lifted the monthly minimum wage for garment workers by 36 percent, to 17,000 taka (about $136), after a wage board vote of 4-2. It is the smallest percentage rise for the sector in four decades, and it came after weeks of street protests that had shut 87 factories in Ashulia, Savar and Gazipur. Workers had demanded 30,000 to 32,000 taka, while factory owners had initially offered 15,000 taka. Union leaders called the outcome 'not respectful', while employers argue that direct labour costs of about 42 cents per garment, above rivals in Vietnam and India, leave margins too thin. Brands are being urged to pay higher prices, and rights groups warn that factories could push unpaid overtime to offset the rise. The outcome matters for the world's second-largest apparel exporter and for the buyers sourcing from it.

Victims' families welcomed the report but were disappointed by parts of the response.

stories.headline: The security of US water systems is even leakier than we thought
stories.claim: Securin report finds US water-system tech vendors carry nearly twice as many vulnerabilities as official records show, with exposed cellular modems a key risk.
stories.summary: US drinking water and industrial water systems are more exposed than official records suggest. A new index from exposure management firm Securin, covering 236 technology vendors, found almost twice as many vulnerabilities as federal databases list, including 20 exploited flaws missing from CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue. Five vendors, led by Rockwell Automation, account for 191 of 376 water-tagged advisories. The more pressing risk is access without exploits: 791 Rockwell MicroLogix 1400 controllers were internet-exposed as of 17 November, and most exposed Rockwell controllers sit on mobile networks via poorly secured cellular modems. The report follows July intrusions, linked by researchers to Iran-affiliated actors, that hit more than 100 water systems across at least 12 states.

Recommended fixes include locating every cellular modem, removing internet exposure and adding MFA gateways.

Adobe also launched Firefly Design in beta, a single workspace for raster, vector, motion, 3D and print design, and previewed local MCP integrations that let third-party AI agents work inside its apps, with a private beta planned for early 2027. The move deepens Adobe's push to position AI agents at the centre of creative software, a key strategic battleground against generative AI rivals.
key_points: Adobe's Creative Agent now powers AI assistants in beta across Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign, After Effects and Frame.io.
The Creative Agent was unveiled at Adobe MAX in Miami Beach on 10 November; features are rolling out now.
Firefly Design, a new beta workspace, combines raster, vector, motion, 3D and print design.
Local MCP integrations let third-party AI agents edit Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere and After Effects files, with a private beta due in early 2027.
Topaz Labs, now owned by Adobe, released Wonder 4 and Image HDR, sold separately.
stories.market_take: A incremental product expansion for Adobe's creative suite; limited direct effect on the share price.

stories.headline: Casa GLS / Filipe Saraiva
stories.claim: Filipe Saraiva's Casa GLS in Ourém is a house split into rotating volumes that each seek their own sun and view.
stories.summary: ArchDaily presents Casa GLS, a house by Filipe Saraiva in Ourém, Portugal, whose design breaks the home into separate volumes that rotate on the site. Each volume is oriented to catch its own sun and landscape view, and the architects argue that the fragmentation shapes the way the household lives. It is a residential architecture project, notable mainly for its design approach rather than for any wider news.

The house is divided into several volumes that rotate on the terrain.
Each volume is oriented to find its own sunlight and landscape.
The architects say the fragmented form shapes the way of living inside.
